In massive machine-type communications, utilizing grant-free access reduces latency and signaling overhead, which are essential advantages. However, this approach poses a challenge, as channel estimation is complicated by user channel uncertainty and potential simultaneous channel estimations. To address this, we propose a framework that leverages the synergy between grant-free access and compressed sensing, as well as a deep learning-based framework. Our results show that these approaches successfully tackle the challenge of multiple machine-type devices transmitting signals without prior scheduling.

A comprehensive comparison is undertaken of different ways to represent the thermodynamic state of moist air by utilizing various thermodynamic potentials. These potentials, which include modified forms of internal energy, enthalpy, Helmholtz free energy, and Gibbs free energy, form the foundation for a systematic method of developing consistent thermodynamic equations of state. A representative theoretical framework is initially presented using internal energy, and a generalization of this formulation for liquid water content is discussed. A detailed comparison of various compressible-liquid models, all based on a theoretical analysis of entropy, highlights similarities among them. A detailed example examination of a proposed energy-based model for moist air reveals that a corresponding equation of state based on the Helmholtz free energy can be derived, and this same framework can be extended to account for liquid water content in a theoretically consistent manner.

We introduce algebraic objects, which we call ideistic monoids and algebraids, to model the properties of idempotent semirings in terms of group objects within the category of pointed sets. By doing so, we establish a direct correspondence between these objects and classical semirings, thus capturing their algebraic essence. Further generalization leads to the concept of double groupoids with actions, which we call ideistic double monoids and algebraids, and demonstrate their equivalence to both classical semirings and poises. Our work lays the groundwork for developing new algebraic structures within the framework of higher algebraic structures, which may ultimately facilitate understanding of higher algebraic structures on motivic rings and their connections to generalized algebraic geometry.

This study explores the feasibility of using confusion networks (derived from a series of top N alternative ASR hypotheses) as a foundation for spoken dialogue systems. A fundamental aspect of spoken dialogue systems involves generating response texts from a series of audio inputs transcribed into text. A comparison was conducted between a current method (sequence-to-sequence models) and an alternative approach (a modified seq2seq model) that takes confusion networks as input. A dataset consisting of 500 utterances from the CoVoST ASR dataset, covering a range of linguistic complexities and languages, was employed for evaluation. Results indicate that the traditional seq2-sequence model outperformed the confusion network-based models, which exhibited relatively low performance on this task.

Semistable coherent sheaves on a complex projective curve are analyzed and their enumerative invariants and moduli space are determined. This work builds upon previous research on the enumerative invariants of stable sheaves.

A critical factor in secret sharing schemes is identifying which groups of participants can access the secret. Among various access structures, the universal access structure stands out as the set of minimal groups capable of accessing the secret, encompassing all possible (n+1)-group combinations where n represents the total number of participants. In this study, we introduce a novel approach to construct a totally symmetric secret sharing scheme for the universal access structure, using a method that allows the scheme to remain consistent across all participants. This approach employs character sums over finite fields, enabling us to achieve constructibility in any prime power size field. Furthermore, our method facilitates the development of efficient protocols for achieving consistent access among all (n+1)-group combinations.

Measuring entanglement between two-qubit systems is crucial in quantum information, optics, and measurement-based computing, but obtaining precise results with statistical efficiency is challenging. We have developed a method to achieve optimal precision in measuring the entanglement of polarization qubits, which can be applied to various contexts. Our approach is based on using a parameter-dependent polarization basis for individual photons, which allows us to calculate the entanglement of two-photon states accurately. We have tested this method experimentally on a non-deterministic two-photon state and found it to be more efficient than previous techniques in terms of both speed and accuracy. We have also used our method to track entanglement in real-time and are exploring its application in dynamic scenarios.

The study of drift wave turbulence in plasmas has been a significant area of research for several decades. Past studies have shown that this type of turbulence is characterized by localized structures known as eddies, which are associated with enhanced magnetic fluctuations. We have used numerical simulations to investigate the relationship between these structures and magnetic fluctuations. Our results indicate that regions within the turbulence, called islands, exhibit significant magnetic activity and are associated with currents flowing through them. We have used a localized version of the drift kinetic gyrofluid model to simulate the evolution of waves and have found that these structures exhibit distinct features in both local and global transport. Our simulations have shown that these localized regions can coexist with areas of turbulent activity, which can affect the transport of particles and heat. Our work has implications for understanding the behavior of plasmas in devices such as tokamaks, where turbulent activity can affect confinement.

Recent studies have explored applying deep learning in Continual Learning.
A key challenge in this area is preventing catastrophic forgetting, which involves
recalling previously seen data when learning new data classes.
Despite its importance, there's a lack of research on its practical feasibility for real-world scenarios.
This paper investigates the feasibility of using the Exponential Moving Average (EMA) method for image classification tasks.
We discovered that by applying EMA to a frozen Exponential Moving Average of a model, we can achieve high accuracy,
even after learning multiple data classes, without falling below the original data's accuracy threshold.
Furthermore, our results demonstrate that EMA-based continual learning surpasses other existing methods in terms of practical feasibility.

As social media platforms grow, so does the issue of hate speech online, which can lead to severe consequences such as mental illness and violence. Although numerous organizations strive to combat hate speech, the problem persists, largely due to the lack of sufficient resources for reporting and moderation. The rapid evolution of hate speech also poses a challenge, as outdated datasets may not accurately reflect its current manifestations. This study presents a new dataset called DeViDa-Hate, which is a large, balanced collection of hateful Hindi comments annotated with their target group and divided into training, validation, and testing subsets. Additionally, we have developed multiple models to classify hate speech and identify its targets, achieving an accuracy of 84.4% on the development set using RoBERTa and ensemble learning techniques. Our findings also include thorough experiments to assess the performance and robustness of the models. Finally, our analysis reveals the limitations of the DeViDa-Hate dataset, highlighting areas for improvement.

We investigate the behavior of large networks of identical, type-I linear neurons with random synaptic connections that can cause inhibition. The neurons follow a Poisson process with a random, unimodal degree distribution, resulting in a finite in-degree for each neuron. By assuming a conditional convergence of the empirical degree distribution to the corresponding mean measure on the space of discrete measures, we establish the existence of a deterministic limit for the time-averaged membrane potential. Building upon this framework, we extend our analysis to characterize oscillations in both temporal and spatial domains. Notably, we find that introducing a broader in-degree distribution can reduce or even suppress oscillations. Our results are further validated using numerical simulations on networks with geometrically distributed degrees.

Recent years have seen significant advancements in algorithm-based software repair, 
driven by cross-disciplinary research. A key focus in this field is on 
automating program repair through search and machine learning (ML) approaches. 
Despite their respective strengths and limitations, integrating ML-generated 
fixes into repair systems remains an open challenge. This study proposes a 
novel solution to this problem by leveraging a Gen. Adv. Net. (GAN) based ML 
method to identify effective bug fixes. A series of experiments conducted on 
real-world code repositories from GitHub demonstrate that the GAN-based method 
outperforms state-of-the-art ML and search-based techniques in generating high 
quality bug fixes.

This study introduces a general capacity region formula for a complex interference channel, applicable to various channel types. It defines a broad metric, called spectral inf-mutual information rate, which characterises the capacity region of complex interference channels. A specific application of this metric is demonstrated for channels with matrix-valued noise, where a partial characterization of the capacity region is achieved. Furthermore, the study shows that the previous capacity region formulas for scalar noise interference channels can be derived as a specific case of this new metric.

The rapid spread of the COVID-19 pandemic has caused a global crisis, with a significant number of deaths and infections. Effective management of the disease requires early identification and treatment to alleviate the burden on healthcare systems. To address this challenge, researchers have developed machine learning models for identifying COVID-19 cases. A study involving 12,620 chest X-ray images found that early detection of the disease is crucial. To improve accuracy, feature enhancement and transfer learning techniques were employed to optimize model performance. By incorporating deep convolutional neural networks, the research team achieved high performance with reduced training time and parameters. Specifically, their best model demonstrated a accuracy of 92.1%, recall of 90.3%, and a F1 score of 91.1%, outperforming other models. This study's source code and dataset are available for further research.

A Graph Neural Network (GNN) is an advanced neural network architecture designed to process graph-based data. Recently, GNNs have been increasingly applied in wireless communication systems, but most existing research has been conducted in fragmented sub-disciplines. This paper aims to consolidate knowledge on GNN applications in wireless systems, detailing theoretical foundations, modeling approaches, and processing graph data in wireless communication systems. Furthermore, it highlights key challenges and provides an overview of potential future research directions and opportunities.

In 2017, Brazil recorded the highest rates of violent crime, including double the average for murders and rapes. To address this, Brazil has been implementing various policies, particularly in the area of public security and urban planning. This study examines the relationship between urban planning policies and homicide rates across Brazil's cities. By correlating data on murders and the characteristics of cities' planning policies, researchers found a stronger relationship between these factors in black communities, which also experience the highest levels of violence. Notably, certain policy areas, including health, education, and public security, show a significant correlation with lower homicide rates in well-policied areas. Conversely, other policy areas, including social protection and transportation, exhibit a weaker relationship with violence.

Optimizing smooth, strongly-convex functions is a critical task in optimization theory.  This paper delves into the convergence properties of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with decreasing step sizes in both deterministic and stochastic settings.  We demonstrate that in a deterministic environment, using an exponentially decreasing step size of 1/t yields a $\mathcal{O}(1/exp(2\alpha t))$ convergence rate in the gradient norm, and this can be improved to a $\mathcal{O}(1/exp(\beta t))$ rate in the objective function value under certain conditions.  Furthermore, we show that when noise in gradients exists, an appropriately chosen step size of 1/exp($\alpha_1 t$) can still achieve a $\mathcal{O}(1/exp(\alpha_2 t))$ convergence rate in the objective function value, and this can be further optimized for the gradient norm with additional modifications.  We also incorporate our analysis into a machine learning context, specifically a least-squares problem, and use our results to prove that SGD with decreasing step sizes can reach an arbitrarily low level of excess risk.  This contrasts existing research on SGD for strongly-convex functions which primarily focuses on $\epsilon$-optimal solutions, and our analysis provides a more refined understanding of the problem's solution quality.

The ability of biological systems to store and process information is a key factor in their adaptability, yet pinpointing the physical mechanisms behind this ability is a complex challenge. To address this, researchers have developed the concept of the memory kernel to pinpoint the specific time frames in which a system's response is influenced by its past. Building upon this, a new approach has been proposed to derive the location of the memory kernel from experimental data, allowing for the derivation of a set of coupled equations that govern the system's evolution, even under non-equilibrium conditions. This theory is tested on a model representing a biological system involved in short-term synaptic plasticity and is further validated by agreement with experimental data on synaptic strength evolution.

Dexterous grasping allows robots to interact with the world in more natural ways, enabling tasks such as manipulating objects and exploring environments. However, replicating dexterous grasping experiences in the physical world is both time-consuming and costly. Our research presents DEXGRASPNET, a comprehensive dataset of more than 100K dexterous grasping instances, which is the largest available dataset of its kind. Built upon an automated pipeline, DEXGRASPNET captures a diverse range of objects and states, complemented by more than 1M synthetic samples. Our dataset serves as a benchmark to evaluate state-of-the-art policies, revealing remarkable advancements in task performance. Moreover, training on DEXGRASPNET yields a remarkable transfer performance of more than 80% across a wide range of physical testing instances of nearly 50K, significantly outperforming simulation-only datasets of similar categories.

A novel approach has been created to develop individual, internal motion maps that can make up for respiratory movements during MRI scans of the abdomen and pelvis. Distinguishing between external movements of the patient's chest and actual internal movements is a problem, so a correction technique using individual internal maps has been developed. A volunteer was used to test a two-step process that involved capturing a series of MRI scans, analyzing the data, and generating a map that could be used to align a motion-compensated image with a target respiratory phase. The results showed that a specific method called PAMoC produced a clearer and more detailed MRI image of a multi-phase scan of a subject's abdomen.

We introduce a novel on-device learning method, incorporating knowledge distillation and low-rank factorization, to rapidly adapt a pre-compressed model for low-data personalization. The process involves two stages: first, a high-rank model is quickly trained on data and subsequently compressed; then, the compressed model is fine-tuned with distillation from the pseudo-labels generated by the model itself. The proposed approach, referred to as Low-Rank Distillation (LRD), is evaluated on a variety of tasks and datasets and demonstrates an improvement in personalization accuracy of 3-11% over existing methods.

Two real-valued functions on a 2D space are considered equivalent if a continuous transformation of that space can be found, which also maps the level sets of one function to those of the other. This is the definition of topological equivalence. We establish a condition under which two continuous, non-constant functions are topologically equivalent, specifically by showing that this occurs when their associated regular foliations are topologically equivalent, a concept we also define in this context. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between these topological properties and the requirement for the equivalence transformation to be a smooth function, a property known as $C^1$. We establish a condition under which this $C^1$ property can be guaranteed, specifically by showing that this occurs when the regular points of the functions are non-degenerate. We discuss a scenario where this condition does not hold, a scenario involving a function with a degenerate regular point. We introduce a new concept, the 'intrinsic equivalence', an equivalence relation that encompasses a stronger form of equivalence between the regular foliations of two functions, and under which intrinsic equivalences can be realized via transformations that are also $C^1$. We establish a condition under which intrinsic equivalences can be realized, a condition that involves a specific type of local symmetry in the critical points of the functions. Ecosystems with sparse vegetation and uneven plant distribution are commonly seen in grazing landscapes, but the effects of this arrangement on grazing patterns are still poorly understood. To investigate this, researchers examined how different plant arrangements influence grazing intensity in a mathematical model of a dry ecosystem. By employing stochastic processes, the study analyzed the distribution of vegetation and grazing in various scenarios, comparing the effects of specific versus general patterns of vegetation spacing. The results indicate that general models of grazing can provide accurate predictions of the effects of biomass loss regardless of the specific plant arrangement. The researchers found that the statistical properties of grazing models, such as the distribution's shape parameter, are crucial in understanding the effects of grazing on vegetation. The study suggests that the outcome of grazing experiments relying on specific plant arrangements may not be applicable to general models of grazing.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch is often utilized to map high-dimensional vectors into a lower-dimensional space with a small margin of error. This algorithm provides an approximation that preserves the Lp norm of each vector. Unfortunately, implementing this algorithm becomes computationally expensive when dealing with vectors containing a range of values, as it typically requires a large number of additional operations to calculate power norms. Our innovation addresses this limitation by reducing the number of additional operations to a constant level, making it applicable for both lq norms where q is greater than 1 and being big-O optimal. This improvement is supported by rigorous error analysis based on advanced concentration inequalities and does not rely on the specific data being analyzed.

A python-based program called pyCMC has been created to execute auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations on chemical systems. pyCMC demonstrates enhanced speed compared to previous Gaussian-based and numerical-based implementations of quantum Monte Carlo, with the aid of highly optimized C code that leverages multithreading, timing data, and scaling benchmarks. The reliability of pyCMC is substantiated by comparing its results to published values in the literature and showing agreement with density functional theory predictions. The pyCMC software is freely accessible through a public GitHub repository.

High-frequency trading algorithms have gained prominence in the financial sector, 
often shrouded in secrecy and controversy. This research explores the impact of 
algorithmic high-frequency trading through the lens of game theory, employing a 
game-theoretic model to assess the effects of HFT on market efficiency and stability.
To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first application of game theory to 
investigate the influence of HFT, a field typically approached through statistical 
analysis. Our goal is to assess whether high-frequency trading contributes to 
systemic risks and market stability, and whether the increased speed of HFT 
algorithms leads to improved outcomes for market participants. Analysis of our 
model suggests that HFT does not yield optimal results, as measured by 
Pareto-optimality, and may even be detrimental to market stability.

We examine a mechanism design problem for selling $k$ items to unit-demand buyers with private valuations for each item, who can bid simultaneously. The first-best optimal mechanism is theoretically determined, under the assumption that the items' valuations are independently and identically distributed according to a general continuous probability distribution. If the items are identical, the distribution of the valuations is a general log-concave distribution. It's shown that the mechanism involves selling one item at a time through a sequential auction, with each auction being a second-price reverse-English auction where the reserve price is set at zero for the first item and a positive value determined by a general formula for subsequent items. It's demonstrated that this mechanism's design can be computed in polynomial time when the distribution of the buyers' valuations is known, utilizing a general algorithm for convex optimization. Furthermore, it's proven that a simple two-item bundle auction can achieve at least half of the expected revenue generated by the optimal mechanism.

To enhance abstractive summarization, we introduce an entity chain that communicates precise information through a non-neural model, which is integrated into the objective function during training based on mutual information. By incorporating these entity chains, which convey detailed context, we anticipate that generated summaries will be more accurate in their representations. Our experiments on two datasets demonstrate our approach's effectiveness in producing high-quality summaries, particularly in scenarios where neural models are typically challenged.

This research presents new sufficient conditions for differentiating multivariable functions. The outcomes extend and refine prior works, particularly those found in Reference 1. It also introduces a specific application, showcasing the practical utility of the results. With an aim to facilitate understanding and enable further research, we have included detailed proofs. The findings are initially stated in a form that employs Lie algebra, which can be translated into a more conventional form at ease.

Human vocal synchronization in social interactions is a crucial indicator of one's cognitive abilities and behavior. This study aims to develop a model that measures similarity in the voices of speakers based on a single sentence, using deep neural networks to capture both acoustic characteristics and fine-grained voice features. A vocal variation dataset has been created to evaluate the effectiveness of our models in learning discriminative voice representations. Furthermore, a large-scale speech dataset called HCS has been compiled to assess the models' ability to generalize across diverse speakers and social contexts. A classification framework based on HCS data has been proposed, which categorizes vocal similarity into various dimensions, including cognitive, behavioral, conversational, and general conversation. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed models outperform existing state-of-the-art methods in audio-visual and audio-based social similarity tasks.

A recent study applied a realizability technique to establish the meaning of a quantum lambda calculus, which results in a multitude of acceptable typing rules, all of equal standing. Building upon this concept, we present a set of sufficient typing rules, which we subsequently prove to have complete coverage. These rules distinctly separate the concepts of objectivity and multiplicity, which were previously conjoined. We also formulate certain denotational constraints that can guarantee the stability of repeated measurements. In contrast to other approaches, our strategy employs a technique utilizing quantum operations to express how multiple instances can be exchanged without external interference.

Calculations of quasiparticle excitation energies are carried out in both the Laughlin and composite fermions systems, featuring either four or ten electrons. Notably, the Laughlin and composite fermions quasiparticle energies of five electrons are found to be identically zero, serving as a local expansion point for systems with six or more electrons. For composite fermions with ten electrons, the quasiparticle energy is obtained by applying this local expansion. Additionally, the quasielectron excitation energy for composite fermions with nine electrons is computed.

In the context of glaciology, particularly for modeling subglacial water flow in large-scale ice sheet simulations, Stokes variational inequalities are relevant. This research focuses on a novel numerical approach based on a mixed finite element method, which accurately handles non-smooth variational inequalities. The proposed approach utilizes neighboring iterations to handle non-differentiability while ensuring optimal convergence for the mixed Stokes problem with a nonlinear boundary condition. We examine the effectiveness of our method through various numerical experiments.

The interplay between a galaxy's star formation rate and its mass loss through the outflow of gas is a crucial aspect of a galaxy's evolution. This study investigates the dynamics of outflowing gas in 11 large samples of starbursting galaxies by analyzing H-alpha and [NII] emission. The researchers found that a significant proportion of a galaxy's star formation rate is carried away by outflowing gas, with the velocity of the outflow being directly proportional to the star formation rate. This relationship can be attributed to the fact that the energy released from the galaxy's supernovae is balanced by the energy required to remove gas from the galaxy. This discovery has significant implications for our understanding of the galaxy's evolution, particularly in the early stages of its formation.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow, we found that the triangular flow exhibits a non-monotonic relationship with centrality. This phenomenon arises from a competition between interplay between anisotropic potential and anisotropic spatial extension, resulting in a less pronounced triangular flow compared to elliptical flow. This similarity in behavior suggests that anisotropic spatial extension and anisotropic interaction among particles are both crucial in determining anisotropic flow.

This paper examines how to coordinate a swarm of robots, focusing on reaching agreement on movement actions. Our approach employs a synchronization method that ensures all robots execute the same commands in a synchronized manner without requiring robot-to-robot communication. This "transparent mechanism" allows robots to share knowledge about their state and environment while executing tasks. We introduce two novel protocols that enable a swarm of robots to achieve consensus on movement without a central leader, using only local interactions. Our findings demonstrate that these mechanisms are applicable to various scenarios, including robots with limited mobility and swarms operating in complex environments.

A novel approach to leveraging the vast amounts of unlabelled videos available online involves using depth maps to generate easy instance segmentation labels for deep neural networks. However, generating high-quality depth maps from these labels is a difficult task. A different strategy focuses on exploring the potential of depth estimation networks without the need for additional training data, using them instead to enhance other tasks such as semantic segmentation. A simple method, based on the assumption that depth estimation networks contain rich low-level visual features, involves using these networks to improve the performance of deep neural networks trained for dense prediction tasks. A range of depth estimation networks, including those generated by self-supervised, unsupervised, or semi-supervised methods, have been found to significantly improve the performance of dense prediction tasks, including semantic segmentation and instance segmentation, without further training. This approach has been shown to provide a simple yet powerful solution for dense prediction tasks, offering an efficient way to utilize the vast amounts of unlabelled videos available online.

Bohr's inequality provides a minimum threshold 'δ' that ensures term-wise absolute value of the power series does not exceed the limit in the open δ disc. In the context of the unit disk, this defines Bohr's radius δ. The threshold δ has been experimentally determined to be no larger than 1/3 and at least 0.36892. A distinct upper bound of 2/3 - 2/9*ln5, 0.3866, was established in the last decade. Researchers are also exploring analogous concepts within bounded convex domains in the complex plane. This research aims to identify the Bohr's phase for a class of such domains, and verify its magnitude is at least 0.36343.

A nonparametric measure of correlation known as Kendall's tau for functional data is investigated. A novel method for computing Kendall's tau is developed, utilizing a between-group distance measure and within a fixed group distance. The method exhibits asymptotic normality when using a between-group distance, whereas the within a fixed group distance yields the conventional Kendall's tau for functional data. Kendall's tau for functional data is demonstrated to be consistent with its scalar data counterpart when using the within a fixed group distance and reducing functional observations to scalars. Additionally, an efficient implementation of the method is provided using a U-statistic framework.

The application of ITS technologies has led to substantial improvements in both traffic management and road safety.  However, to create a truly intelligent transportation system, it is necessary to incorporate real-time data from various sources such as vehicles, sensors, and cameras.  The large volume of data generated by these sources poses a challenge, as it is difficult to transmit this data to the central server.  To address this challenge, Edge Intelligence Systems have been introduced to facilitate a seamless flow of data between Edge Devices and Central Servers.  To further enhance the efficiency of ITS, this research proposes a novel Edge Intelligence System for Intelligent Transportation Systems (EIS-ITS), which enables Central Servers to efficiently distribute tasks to Edge Devices and receive processed data in return.  Furthermore, to improve the overall performance of EIS-ITS, a Task Scheduling Algorithm for Edge Intelligence Transportation System (TSAEITS) has been developed to optimize the execution of models on multiple Edge Devices.  The simulation results indicate that the proposed TSAREITS algorithm outperforms existing approaches, specifically by achieving a response time of 1.5s and an accuracy of 94%.

This study focuses on the application of the Euler characteristic in topological data analysis, particularly for complex structures such as x-ray convex bodies and their related homological objects, including intersection bodies, star bodies, body cones, and their associated kernels.

Our analysis focuses on an adjusted predator-prey model, incorporating a type II functional response and the Bazykin effect. This simplified model captures key features of population dynamics, including the coexistence of stable equilibrium points, the Aleeffect, temporary oscillations, and the risk of species extinction. A comprehensive understanding of the new model's phase plane and temporal behavior is provided.

The Hirsch Conjecture proposes a relationship between the number of facets of a d-dimensional polytope and its diameter, which is thought to be at most d minus the difference between the number of facets of the polytope and the number of vertices of a d-dimensional simplex. This note provides evidence for a modified version of this conjecture, showing that it holds true if the number of edges connecting the maximum number of faces is at least d minus the difference between the number of facets of the polytope and the number of vertices of a d-dimensional simplex. This modified version is proven using modified versions of Hirsch's algorithm, which is a proposed algorithm for finding the shortest path between two vertices of a polytope, and Hirsch's algorithm for linear programming.

We explore in an associative ring R with identity, the scarcity of k-torsion in the NK1GQ(R), which is a graded Q-series of nil-groups. This investigation focuses on an algebra Q and its image in the ring R under an algebra homomorphism.

This paper undertakes a thorough comparison of the comprehensive, off-shell computation for pp -> ttj events, incorporating single and double weak corrections, with a commonly used method of addressing these events, which involves integrating with the leading order process, including non-resonant and off-shell effects. Our findings indicate that the approach of adding with the leading order process significantly underestimates the off-shell and non-resonant contributions, resulting in errors of up to 20-30% for cross sections and p-T distributions, and over 50% tail events for top quark transverse momentum distributions above 500 GeV.

The susceptibility of facial recognition systems to fraudulent attacks poses a significant threat to systems that rely on face matching for security purposes. A particular form of attack, which involves the use of 3D-printed masks to deceive facial recognition systems, is a major concern. While several approaches have been proposed to mitigate this threat, they often suffer from high computational costs and limited scope. In this paper, a more practical solution is presented, which uses 3D depth data to detect malicious masks. The proposed method leverages point cloud data and convolutional networks to distinguish between masks and normal human faces. The method is evaluated on two public datasets and the newly created DeepFakeMaskNet dataset, which consists of images of deep-faked masks. The results show that the proposed method outperforms the state-of-the-art in 3D depth data and is more efficient than other approaches. The method is also shown to achieve a level of accuracy comparable to that of state-of-the-art techniques in RGB-based approaches, but with lower computational costs.

The ability to apply supervised learning principles to real-world data is the key to developing intelligent systems, but in the context of autonomous vehicles, a major hurdle arises from the need for vast amounts of high-resolution sensor data, which is expensive and time-consuming to collect. This document outlines a solution to overcome this challenge by utilizing synthetic data to train perception systems for autonomous vehicles. It begins by addressing the limitations of current sensor data and then discusses various approaches to generating realistic data, including computer vision techniques and advanced graphics methods. Furthermore, it highlights the importance of generating data that accurately represents specific driving scenarios and provides a framework for evaluating the effectiveness of synthetic training data through targeted assessments.

Evolutionary algorithms with parallel processing can search more efficiently and in parallel, but their efficiency might be reduced due to unequal time spent on evaluation by different threads. To address this issue, a new thread scheduling method, called the Bounding Thread Scheduling (BTS) strategy, is proposed for use in parallel differential evolution. Under this strategy, threads are allocated within a predetermined range of population indices, resulting in minimized search time disparity among threads. We investigate the properties of BTS and demonstrate its implementation. Experimental results show improved convergence and fairness among threads when using BTS compared to traditional scheduling methods.

The concept of an effective Floquet Hamiltonian, derived from the Floquet generator, has been criticized for failing to accurately describe the dynamics of periodically driven quantum systems, particularly in regions where two distinct phases of the Floquet generator exist. These phases, previously overlooked, correspond to smoothly connected yet qualitatively different Floquet generators, giving rise to significant differences in dynamics over multiple driving periods. A proposed solution is to develop a more effective effective time-independent Floquet generator, capable of capturing the dynamics over a finite number of driving periods, even though this effective generator depends on the duration of driving and may not correspond to any physical system.

Our investigation of CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ for $0 < x < 1$ reveals a complex interplay between magnetic properties and electronic behavior. Magnetic measurements and analysis of the specific heat indicate that compounds with $x > 0.6$ exhibit long-range antiferromagnetic order. In contrast, the residual heat capacity at $T = 0$ is substantial in the paramagnetic regime, suggesting the presence of a quantum critical point near $x_c = 0.6$. A comprehensive analysis of electrical resistivity, Seebeck coefficient, Hall coefficient, and the Hertz-Millis model of hybridized quantum criticality indicates that $x_c$ is likely close to $x = 0.65$.

The absorption of hydrogen I (HINSA) has been detected in a region of high-mass star formation near a massive molecular cloud core. Researchers used a sensitive 21 cm radio telescope to study the characteristics of this phenomenon in detail. By examining the characteristics of the HINSA in relation to the massive protostar, scientists discovered significant evidence of an inward motion. Furthermore, they found that the strength of the HINSA is directly linked to the temperature of the surrounding environment. These findings suggest that the HINSA can be used to identify areas of gravitational instability and to understand the processes of gravitational fragmentation.

These findings have the further implication of proving the validity of the polynomial approximation theorem for these transformations, which also corresponds to the occurrence of the open set condition in this context.

It is widely acknowledged that deep neural networks excel at capturing intricate patterns within a dataset, but they often falter when faced with generalized tasks due to their reliance on dataset-specific features. Current methods primarily focus on modifying network parameters to enhance model adaptability, whereas our approach targets the data itself by introducing a new representation that mitigates the risk of overfitting to noisy features. Our method involves converting input data into a latent space, where a self-supervised task encourages the network to extract meaningful features, ultimately leading to enhanced model performance across diverse benchmark datasets, including images, speech, and time-series data.

Despite growing interest in explaining Graph Neural Network predictions, existing methods have shortcomings. They tend to be inaccurate, inefficient, and struggle with complex graph structures, particularly when graph components interact extensively. To address these issues, we developed an innovative method that focuses on identifying significant nodes within selected subgraphs. This approach combines a perturbation technique with a dynamic subgraph selector to optimize explanations. To further improve efficiency, we integrated a neural mechanism to quickly identify significant nodes. The proposed framework is versatile, applicable not only to node and link prediction tasks but also to dynamic graph models.
